summary: Describes TSIG, a way to authenticate DNS transactions using a shared secret and a one-way hash. It can verify that dynamic updates to a zone come from an approved client, or that responses come from an approved name server. How the secrets are distributed is left to the network administrator.

plainLanguage.summary: TSIG lets two DNS systems use a shared secret to check who sent a message and whether it changed. RFC 8945 specifies the record format, how each side checks it, and which hash algorithms implementations must support.

subtitle: Authenticate DNS requests and responses with a shared secret and a keyed hash.

tldr.problem: DNS updates, responses, and zone transfers may need proof that a message came from an approved party and was not changed in transit.
tldr.mechanism: Two parties configure a key and algorithm in advance. The sender calculates a keyed hash over the DNS message and TSIG variables, then places the result in a TSIG record.
tldr.outcome: RFC 8945 is an Internet Standard that replaces RFC 2845 and RFC 4635. It changes the order of TSIG checks to prevent a server from signing a reply using an unvalidated request MAC.

facts.label: Minimum MAC length
facts.value: Larger of 10 octets and half the hash length

today: RFC 8945 is an Internet Standard published in November 2020. It obsoletes RFC 2845 and RFC 4635.

sections.title: What TSIG Protects
sections.content:
Secret Key Transaction Authentication for the Domain Name System (DNS), called TSIG, provides authentication and integrity checks between two DNS entities that share a secret key. It can authenticate DNS update requests and responses, and it can protect zone transfers, including glue records.

The parties must agree on the key and algorithm before using TSIG. The agreement and secret distribution are outside this RFC; the document expects an administrator to configure clients and servers. Shared-key management becomes difficult as the number of parties grows, so the RFC describes TSIG as suitable for pairs that communicate with a limited number of peers.
sections.plainLanguage: TSIG lets two DNS systems check that a message came from the other system and was not changed. They must already share a key and agree on a hash algorithm.

sections.title: The TSIG Record
sections.content:
TSIG is a meta-resource record with type code 250. It applies to one DNS transaction, must not be cached, and is discarded after the message is checked. In a message, the TSIG record must be the last record in the additional section. Its class is ANY, its TTL is zero, and its name identifies the key.

The record carries an algorithm name, a 48-bit signing time, a 16-bit Fudge interval, the MAC length and value, the original DNS message ID, an error code, and optional other data. A BADTIME response can use the other-data field to carry the server's current time. The TSIG error values defined here include BADSIG, BADKEY, BADTIME, and BADTRUNC.
sections.plainLanguage: The record names the key and algorithm, records when the message was signed, and carries the check value. It also carries error details when authentication fails.

sections.title: How TSIG Calculates the MAC
sections.content:
A message authentication code (MAC) is a keyed hash used to check a message. TSIG uses a Hashed Message Authentication Code (HMAC) algorithm. For a request, it calculates the MAC from the DNS message and TSIG variables; for a response, it also includes the validated request MAC. The data are hashed in wire format as one continuous sequence.

The sender calculates the MAC before adding the TSIG record and before increasing the additional-record count. The receiver removes the TSIG record, adjusts that count, and restores the original message ID for verification when needed. The signing time and Fudge interval are included in the calculation so an attacker cannot change those values without invalidating the MAC.
sections.plainLanguage: The sender computes a check value from the DNS message, key-related fields, and time values. A response also depends on the validated check value from the request.

sections.title: Checking Requests and Responses
sections.content:
A client appends one TSIG record to a signed request and keeps the key name and MAC while it waits. The server checks the key first, then the MAC, time values, and local truncation policy. An unknown key or invalid MAC produces an unsigned error; a time error can produce a signed BADTIME response.

A client expecting a signed response should not accept an unsigned or unverifiable answer as valid. For a multi-message TCP response, such as a zone transfer, the client must verify the first and last messages and may accept up to 99 intermediary messages without TSIG. If a TSIG check fails on the connection, the client must close it.
sections.plainLanguage: The server checks the key, message check value, time, and permitted check length in that order. A client that expects authentication rejects a response it cannot verify.

sections.title: Hash Algorithms and Truncated MACs
sections.content:
An implementation supporting TSIG must implement HMAC SHA1 and HMAC SHA256. The RFC recommends HMAC SHA256 and says existing HMAC SHA1 use should be replaced with HMAC SHA256 or another SHA-2 algorithm. HMAC-MD5 may be implemented, but must not be used.

A MAC may contain the leading octets of a hash output. A received MAC longer than the hash output, or shorter than the larger of 10 octets and half the hash length, causes the DNS message to be dropped with FORMERR, except for specified error responses. Local policy sets any stricter minimum length.
sections.plainLanguage: TSIG implementations must support HMAC SHA1 and HMAC SHA256, but the RFC recommends SHA256. A shortened check value still has to meet the RFC's minimum length rule.

sections.title: Security and the Revision
sections.content:
TSIG can authenticate communication between two systems while their shared secret remains protected. The key should not be shared by more than two entities, because any holder could impersonate another. TSIG authenticates the transmission, not the original source data. A Fudge interval that is too large can allow replay; one that is too small can reject messages because of clock differences or delays. The recommended interval in most situations is 300 seconds.

This revision fixes an ordering problem in RFC 2845. Some implementations checked the request time before validating its MAC and could use an invalid request MAC in a signed reply. RFC 8945 requires the server to validate the request MAC before the time check; until then, any answer must be unsigned.
sections.plainLanguage: Protect the shared key, because anyone who has it can impersonate its other holder. The revised rules require a server to check a request's MAC before using it to sign a reply.
